analysis.one_liner: Taxes billionaire wealth at 5% a year to fund health care, child care, housing, and teacher pay.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with 7 cosponsors, the bill was sent to four House committees and has seen no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put an annual 5% tax on the net assets of any household holding more than $1 billion, and use the money for a wide list of benefits aimed at working families: a $3,000-per-person rebate payment, an end to the income cap on Affordable Care Act premium subsidies plus repeal of the health cuts in the 2025 reconciliation law, Medicare coverage of dental, hearing, and vision care, roughly $85.6 billion a year for affordable housing, a guaranteed child care entitlement for families with children under 6, a $60,000 minimum salary for public school teachers, and expanded home care funding. It also requires the IRS to audit at least half of the households paying the new tax each year and builds a registry of large owners' assets. The bill has not moved since it was referred to four committees on the day it was introduced.
analysis.who_benefits: Nearly every group at ordinary incomes gains something: every household would receive a $3,000-per-person rebate ($6,000 married, plus $3,000 per child) for 2026; the roughly 60 million people on Medicare would get dental, hearing, and vision coverage starting in 2028; ACA marketplace enrollees above 400% of the poverty line would become newly eligible for premium subsidies and everyone's subsidy would grow; families with young children under 250% of state median income would be entitled to child care; renters gain from $85.6 billion a year for the Housing Trust Fund; every public school teacher would be guaranteed at least $60,000; and Medicaid home care recipients and their aides gain from permanent home- and community-based care investments. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working families, Medicare enrollees, teachers, renters

how_it_helps.text: Any individual or trust with net assets over $1 billion would owe 5% of that net value annually, including on unrealized holdings like company shares, with a 60% rate applied to covered expatriates who renounce citizenship, and the threshold rises with inflation.
The bill directs the IRS to audit at least half of the households that pay the wealth tax each year and funds enforcement with 1% of the tax's revenue.
Households would receive 2026 'affordability rebates' of $3,000 per person ($6,000 per joint return) plus $3,000 per dependent, reusing the 2021 stimulus payment mechanism.

The bill would repeal the health provisions of the 2025 reconciliation law (Public Law 119-21) and remove the 400%-of-poverty income cap on ACA premium tax credits, capping what enrollees pay on a sliding scale that tops out at 8.5% of income.

Medicare would cover dental care, hearing aids, and eyeglasses and routine eye exams starting in 2028, with the added cost to seniors' Part B premiums phased in through 2031 so the new coverage does not cause a sudden premium spike.
The bill authorizes $85.647 billion per year for fiscal 2026 through 2035 for the Housing Trust Fund, which builds and preserves affordable housing for extremely low-income households.

Every child under 6 in a family under 250% of state median income would be entitled to child care through certificates parents can spend at licensed providers, with federal payments sized to providers' actual costs including teacher wages.
The federal government would guarantee a minimum $60,000 annual salary for every public school teacher in the United States.

The bill permanently extends Medicaid spousal impoverishment protections for home- and community-based services and makes the Money Follows the Person demonstration permanent, so people needing long-term care can stay at home without a spouse being driven into poverty.

analysis.who_pays: Households and trusts with more than $1 billion in net assets, who would owe 5% of their net worth every year on top of existing income taxes, which the bill bars them from deducting. Wealthy individuals who renounce their citizenship would owe 60% on the way out. Some owners of large illiquid businesses would need to value hard-to-price assets annually and could face pressure to sell assets or borrow to pay a tax on wealth they have not yet converted to cash.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households with over $1 billion in assets

drawbacks.text: A 5% annual tax on unrealized asset value would force the very largest asset owners to value private companies, art, and other hard-to-price holdings every year, and some would face cash demands on gains they have never sold, raising administrative complexity and legal challenges over whether such a tax is constitutional without apportionment.

The bill's biggest spending items are open-ended: the child care entitlement is funded with 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal 2026 and every year after, so the total cost depends entirely on how large the wealth tax revenue turns out to be.

The Medicare dental fee schedule is set at 70% of the national median private fee, and hearing aids and eyeglasses would be subject to competitive bidding capped at federal supply schedule rates, so some dentists, hearing aid dealers, and eyewear sellers could be paid less per service than they receive privately, though the new Medicare payer pool would be far larger.

The bill would create a federal registry of assets owned by covered taxpayers, including closely held business shares, digital assets, and real estate, which privacy-minded critics would call an intrusive expansion of government tracking of personal wealth.

Requiring audits of at least half of wealth-tax payers every year is an enforcement commitment the IRS has never approached for any taxpayer group, and its feasibility depends on sustained funding that future Congresses could cut.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and broadly shared: cash payments, new Medicare coverage, universal child care for young children, a teacher salary floor, and housing money, all paid for by a narrow tax on roughly the several thousand wealthiest households. The costs are real but largely administrative and transitional: valuation complexity, liquidity pressure for owners of large private companies, likely court challenges to the tax's constitutionality, and open-ended spending commitments that depend on the tax actually raising enough. As written, the design is aggressive but the targeting is clear — the burden falls on the top sliver of wealth and the benefits flow to ordinary families.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees, including Ways and Means, on the day it was introduced, and none has taken it up; with the 119th Congress in session until January 2027, it is waiting and shows no signs of moving.

narrative.text: Ro Khanna introduced the bill on March 3, 2026, and it was referred that same day to the Ways and Means Committee and three other committees, with the Speaker to decide which committee handles which provisions.
Seven House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote since the initial referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost anything yet because the bill has not been acted on; households with over $1 billion in net assets are better off for now simply because the tax has not advanced toward a vote.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 3, 2026, combining a 5% annual tax on billionaire wealth with a package of health, child care, housing, and teacher-pay spending.

for.name: 7 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican or independent did.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: First-referral committee, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Has held no hearing or markup on the bill since it was referred on March 3, 2026; the committee's action history ends at the referral.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.what_they_did: Controls whether the bill ever receives committee consideration; no markup has been scheduled.

against.name: Speaker Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to four committees at once, splitting it so no single committee had full control of its fate, and has not brought it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 7 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican joined, and a tax on billionaire wealth faces opposition from a House Republican majority that controls the committees and the floor calendar.

industries.note: Households with over $1 billion in net assets would owe 5% of that value every year on top of income taxes, with no deduction against income tax and a 60% exit rate for those renouncing citizenship. Their interest in stopping the bill runs directly against the benefits funded by it.

Removing the 400%-of-poverty cap on premium tax credits and capping premiums at 8.5% of income would channel larger subsidies through private marketplace plans, adding customers. Insurers' interest here runs alongside the public's, but the design keeps them the permanent middleman for subsidized coverage.

Medicare dental coverage creates a vast new payer pool for dental care, but the fee schedule is set at 70% of the national median private fee with productivity adjustments, so participation could mean lower per-service payments than private insurers pay.

industries.industry: Hearing aid dispensers, audiologists, and manufacturers
industries.note: Medicare coverage of hearing aids and hearing exams opens a large new market and lets licensed dispensers bill directly, but payment is capped at federal supply schedule rates and subject to competitive bidding by 2031, pressuring prices.

Medicare would cover routine eye exams and one pair of eyeglasses every two years, a new market, but eyeglass payments would be capped at federal supply schedule rates and put to competitive bidding by 2030.

industries.industry: Child care providers and early education workers
industries.note: A universal entitlement for children under 6 would guarantee every eligible family a certificate, and state payment rates must be set to cover providers' actual costs including staff wages, raising revenue and pay across the sector.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and long-term care workforce
industries.note: Planning grants, quality funding, and permanent extension of spousal impoverishment protections and Money Follows the Person would channel more Medicaid money into home- and community-based services.
$85.647 billion a year for a decade through the Housing Trust Fund would fund construction and preservation of housing for the lowest-income renters.

industries.industry: Owners of large closely held businesses
industries.note: Any owner over the $1 billion threshold would have to report and value closely held business interests annually under new IRS rules, and pay tax on value without selling; related children's assets count toward the owner's total.

analysis.trajectory: With only 7 cosponsors out of 217 House Democrats and no Republican support, and the bill sitting with a Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee that has taken no action, the realistic path is that it dies in committee when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. Wealth tax bills introduced in past Congresses have consistently never reached the floor. A reimplementation of the same ideas would require a change in House control.
